title: Mathematicians are furious over an Anthropic researcher's joke about a 250,000-page proof
excerpt: Levent Alpöge said that he proved the Riemann Hypothesis in 250,000 pages using AI. On Monday, he clarified that the page count was a "joke."
content_html:
By Henry Chandonnet

You're currently following this author! Click to unsubscribe from email alerts.

2026-11-24T17:07:20.811Z

Mathematicians aren't in a joking mood these days. Just look at the latest drama in AI math.

It started when Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge said that his proof's code was "full of garbage," but that the math still checks out.

Alpöge said that he proved the Riemann Hypothesis, one of the biggest unsolved problems in mathematics, last week using Claude. Mathematicians told Business Insider that it would be an "extremely big deal," but that they were still checking Alpöge's work.

One challenge: Alpöge's published proof was long. In a footnote to his remark, he wrote that the human-readable version of the proof was over 250,000 pages long, which "amused" him.

The page count appalled onlookers. Gary Marcus called the length "hardly elegant," while other blogs went with "math slop," a harsher invective. "Who is going to read that 250k pages file?" one Redditor asked.

On Monday, Alpöge clarified in post titled "Stupid things I did" that the length was a "joke."

"I find big number extremely hilarious," he wrote on X. "People ran with it unfortunately and I didn't feel like talking on social media in the days after the announcement, though I did have a good time with the memes. Sorry!!!"

Alpöge said that he didn't feel comfortable having "any slop writeup" attached to the proof, so he relied on Lean, the mathematical programming language and theorem prover, instead. Other mathematicians have tested out that formal, computer-centered proof — itself around 17 million lines of code — and so far it appears to be sound.

The joke doesn't invalidate his proof, and he made clear that the Lean code still complies, even if it's overlong.

Stupid things I did:
1. 250,000+ pages was a joke guys!, I find big number extremely hilarious. I tried to make it clear by the level of pedantry of the reals total ordered statement in the main theorem, but people ran with it unfortunately and I didn’t feel like talking on…

— levent (@__alpoge__) November 23, 2026

Mathematicians, who were already reeling from how AI has made several sudden and shocking discoveries in their field, didn't take the joke well. Commenters called him "unprofessional" and told him to hire a communications manager.

"There's no need to kill trust in mathematics and science as a whole with this kind of marketing hype and scam," wrote one mathematician. "They're already dying without it."

Scott Armstrong, a researcher at Sorbonne University, explained on X that asking an AI agent to assemble a proof in a "pedantic" language like Lean, and then asking it to translate to "natural" language, could multiply the page count by 10.

The result would be "hideously long" and "hilarious," Armstrong wrote. For those who didn't find Alpöge's joke funny, Armstrong said: "I don't know what to tell you."

Alpöge was more accepting of the feedback.

"All criticism of such garbage is totally reasonable and accepted," he wrote. "I should have cleaned it up but it was randomly difficult to for various strange reasons. Mea culpa…"
